 ## Search results
NextItNet’s foundation is residual causal dilated convolution: expanding receptive fields captures short- and long-range dependencies without pooling ([original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163)). Searches found adjacent 2023–2026 work rather than a directly verified time-gated, adaptive-receptive-field NextItNet successor. GCTN (2023) combines time-interval modeling with personalized gating, although its graph/category components exceed this task’s available inputs ([paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2023.119510)). FADC (CVPR 2024) demonstrates input-dependent dilation in vision; useful architectural inspiration, but no evidence of recommendation gains ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05369)). HeteroTempRec (2026) adaptively balances immediate and long-term preferences, but uses a CNN–Transformer architecture rather than the required NextItNet backbone ([paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2025.122703)).

A compatible research hypothesis is to add jointly trained gates inside NextItNet residual blocks, weighting small versus large causal dilation paths using prefix features and observed log-scaled timestamp gaps. Large gaps could attenuate stale context; coherent recent interactions could favor shorter receptive fields. Temporal gating has recommendation precedent in time-aware attentive memory networks, although that work predates the requested period and uses a different backbone ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598)). This adaptation remains an untested proposal: keep every gate causal, mask padding throughout, read the final nonpadding position, and use one jointly trained network/checkpoint per category. Compare fixed dilation, content-only gating, and timestamp-conditioned gating using the pinned macro validation HR@10; no published result establishes improvement on this benchmark.

---

Recent work supports combining item text with collaborative signals, but does not establish a ready-made solution under the no-pretraining constraint. [Recformer (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13731) jointly learns language and sequential recommendation representations, using a Transformer backbone. [TედRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18166) identifies limitations of directly adding text and ID embeddings; its sequence-level Fourier fusion is equivalent to contextual convolution. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) incorporates titles, descriptions and reviews through BERT, with reviews contributing most—its reported gains therefore do not directly transfer to this task’s available inputs or initialization restrictions.

Product text can describe functionality, but complementarity and substitution require careful supervision. [Amazon’s SIGIR 2023 substitute model](https://www.amazon.science/publications/a-transformer-based-substitute-recommendation-model-incorporating-weakly-supervised-customer-behavior-data) matches title/description text while denoising behavioral supervision; it does not establish that semantic similarity alone identifies substitutes. A constraint-compatible hypothesis, rather than a demonstrated result from these papers: randomly initialize a small word/subword embedding encoder with pooling or text CNN, learn a gated residual fusion with item-ID embeddings, and jointly optimize it inside the existing causal NextItNet using next-item supervision. Shared text parameters could help sparse items, while the gate limits noisy descriptions. Preserve one network/checkpoint per category; treat compatibility and purchase intent as latent hypotheses, never observed labels. Validate any benefit through the fixed macro HR@10 protocol.

---

Sampled softmax provides competition against multiple negatives and naturally concentrates gradients on high-scoring mistakes; temperature controls this emphasis, with overly aggressive settings risking domination by a few difficult negatives. The 2024 [sampled-softmax analysis](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) supports ranking benefits but does not establish gains for NextItNet on Electronics. A separate [2024 sequential-recommendation comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276), covering random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling, found dataset-dependent tradeoffs: uniform sampling favored head items, while popularity-based sampling could improve balance at lower overall accuracy. [R²NS, WWW 2026](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports that introducing hard negatives too early can underperform uniform sampling; uniform warm-up followed by progressively harder, stochastic selection improves robustness.

False-negative safeguards matter because high-scoring unobserved items may be genuine future positives. [EMM, 2026](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026004090) combines hard/random negatives with ID exclusion and similarity-window filtering, although its evidence concerns graph contrastive recommendation rather than NextItNet. Practical hypothesis for this task: retain one NextItNet per category; compare uniform multi-negative sampled softmax against uniform warm-up followed by a modest hard/uniform mixture. Exclude padding, targets and known training positives; sample stochastically among difficult candidates rather than always choosing the maximum. Treat similarity filtering as an ablation, since it can remove useful distinctions.
